clinicalPearls: Presents as one or more well-defined, red-brown to violaceous papules, plaques or nodules, most often on the face of middle-aged adults
Prominent, dilated follicular openings (accentuated ostia) over the surface are a helpful clinical clue
Despite the name it is a localised chronic fibrosing vasculitis of the skin and is unrelated to systemic granulomatous disease
Lesions are usually asymptomatic, persistent and cosmetically bothersome, and sun-exposed facial skin is typically affected
Biopsy shows a dense mixed dermal infiltrate rich in eosinophils and neutrophils with a leucocytoclastic vasculitis and a characteristic Grenz zone of uninvolved papillary dermis
Later lesions show perivascular fibrosis and haemosiderin deposition reflecting the chronic vascular injury
It is often resistant to treatment; options include topical or intralesional corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, dapsone, laser and surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Granuloma faciale is a chronic, localised leucocytoclastic vasculitis of the skin in which recurrent immune-complex-mediated injury to small dermal vessels drives a persistent, eosinophil- and neutrophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate. Repeated vascular damage leads to fibrinoid change, extravasation of red cells with haemosiderin deposition and, over time, perivascular and dermal fibrosis. A narrow Grenz zone of spared papillary dermis separates the infiltrate from the epidermis. The tendency for sun-exposed facial skin to be affected suggests actinic factors may contribute to its localisation.
additionalDifferentials: Fixed drug eruption or persistent arthropod reaction
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing leucocytoclastic vasculitis with eosinophils and a Grenz zone
Direct immunofluorescence, which may show immunoreactant deposition around vessels
Full blood count including eosinophil count
Investigations to exclude sarcoidosis or lupus when clinically suggested
Dermoscopy to highlight dilated follicular openings and vascular features
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration or atypical features prompting exclusion of cutaneous lymphoma or malignancy
Extrafacial or multiple lesions raising diagnostic doubt
Failure to respond to standard therapies over prolonged follow-up
Diagnostic uncertainty overlapping with systemic granulomatous disease
reference.prognosis: Granuloma faciale is a benign but persistent and often treatment-resistant condition; lesions rarely resolve spontaneously and tend to recur after treatment, so management is frequently aimed at cosmetic improvement rather than cure.
pitfalls: Assuming the name implies systemic granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis
Mistaking it clinically for rosacea, lupus or a skin tumour without biopsy
Expecting a rapid or durable response, given its refractory nature
Overlooking cutaneous lymphoma in the histological differential
